title: Subprocessor onboarding tolerances — negotiation scratchpad
content:
Notes to self / quick scratch (subprocessors onboarding tolerances)

Context:
- Customer asking for: 48h notification + opt-out for new subprocessors (any change) + right to audit all subprocessors.
- Standard internal posture: notify 10 days prior for material subprocessors; provide list quarterly; SOC2 or equivalent for security-critical subprocessors; confirm flowdown of data obligations.
- Key tradeoff: operational cadence vs customer trust. Short notice windows kill ops (we use multiple small infra providers + SaaS tooling).

Primary risks to flag:
- P1: Immediate opt-out (customer can refuse new subprocessor) -> could require contract changes, breaks autoscaling/region failover.
- P2: Unrestricted audit right (customer audits vendor directly) -> vendor pushback, requires ID redaction, purpose/notice/cost allocation.
- P3: Broad "any change" definition (includes non-material infra updates) -> creates noise.

Negotiation anchors (what we propose):
1) Notification window: 10 business days for material subprocessors; 30 days for others via consolidated quarterly list (we can compromise to 7 business days for material in high-security customers).
2) Opt-out: limited to material processors with documented security gaps; opt-out must be exercised within 5 business days of notice and requires mitigation plan + temporary suspension clause.
3) Audit rights: right to request summary SOC/ISO attestation and redacted audit report. On-site/customer-directed audits allowed only with pre-approval, scoped, and cost recovery.
4) Flowdown: subprocessor must be bound by substantially similar obligations; we certify flowdown in writing and provide sample contract template on request.
5) Data residency: subprocessors may process data outside the EU/US only if approved prior and adequately secured (we accept approved cloud vendors list).

Practical redline language (editable) — start conservative, then soften:
- Customer request: "Supplier will notify Customer of any new subprocessor within 48 hours and Customer may object; if Customer objects, Supplier will not engage the subprocessor for that Customer's data."

- Proposed counter (balanced): "Supplier will provide written notice of any new subprocessor that will process Customer Data at least ten (10) business days prior to engagement. Customer shall have five (5) business days from receipt of such notice to reasonably object in writing if Customer reasonably believes the proposed subprocessor presents an unacceptable risk to Customer Data. In the event of a timely objection, the parties will meet in good faith to discuss mitigation; if no mitigation acceptable to Customer is available, either party may suspend the transfer of Customer Data to the proposed subprocessor pending alternative arrangements. 
Note: objections shall be specific and supported by objective evidence; routine operational changes (maintenance, minor vendor upgrades) are excluded from the definition of 'new subprocessor'."

- Audit right language (counter): "Supplier will make available to Customer evidence of Supplier's selection and oversight of its subprocessors, including recent third-party security attestations (e.g., SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001) and summary audit reports, subject to reasonable confidentiality measures. Customer may request an on-site or vendor-directed audit only where Customer demonstrates a reasonable basis for concern and after failing to obtain satisfactory responses to written inquiries; any such audit shall be subject to mutual agreement on scope, timing and a cost-sharing arrangement."

Escalation / fallback positions: 
- If customer insists on 48h + open opt-out: escalate to sales + CSM; offer a risk-based carveout (e.g., only for data classified as Highly Confidential/regulated) and additional contractual protections (higher indemnity cap for breaches caused by subprocessor).
- If customer insists on unlimited on-site audits: offer a vendor-managed witness-only audit or require auditor NDA + cost recovery + audit scope cap.

Checklist for negotiation call:
- Ask: what types of subprocessors are they most worried about? infra (cloud), analytics, logging, CDNs, support tools?
- Confirm whether customer expects per-change notice (bad) or quarterly list + material change alerts (better).
- Walk through our vendor approval process + attestation cadence (SOC2 every 12 months; pen test annually).
- Offer: early-access to our approved vendor list + data flow diagram for their account.

Open questions / research items:
- What is our internal threshold for 'material subprocessor'? (by data exposure, number of routed tokens, role in processing). Need product input from Infra. 
- Which of our small vendors can produce SOC2? If not, can we provide supplementary controls? Ask SRE and procurement.
- Precedent: find 3 customer contracts where we accepted 7-day notice + limited opt-out. Link examples.

Sample talking points (concise for AE/SE):
- "We want to be transparent about changes; we can provide a quarterly list and 10 business days notice for anything that meaningfully affects your data. This keeps your right to object while allowing us to operate critical infrastructure.
- "For heightened concerns, we'll agree to additional attestations or a scoped audit rather than blanket on-site rights — it's faster and preserves confidentiality of our vendor relationships."

Fallback legal arguments to defend our posture:
- Unlimited on-site audits undermine our contractual commitments to other customers and expose vendor intellectual property and non-customer data.
- Immediate opt-out for any change can make high-availability features (regional failover) impossible to deliver.
- Requiring SOC2 for every tiny tool is disproportionate; instead require reasonable security controls + mitigation plan for non-cert vendors.

Action items (owners):
- Asha: pull 3 precedent contracts with similar language (due EOD).
- Liam: confirm which infra subs (CDN, metrics, logging) have SOC2 by next Tue.
- Sofia: draft a short playbook email + 2 alternate redlines (conservative / permissive) for AE to use.

Notes to self: keep this doc informal; intended to be a quick-reference for negotiations and for handing to product/infra/legal for input. Save a cleaned version if we land an acceptable compromise.

End of scratchpad.
